claims.text: The starting material is a near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi alloy.
Solution-annealed near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has a nominally single-phase FCC-like microstructure.
Near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi contains partial short-range ordering among Ti, Ni, and Co.
Short-range order can affect stacking-fault energy and the activation barrier for dislocation motion in multicomponent alloys.
Ti-containing short-range order affects local dislocation-core structures in CoCrFeNiTi.
Short-range chemical ordering in CoCrFeNiTi reduces its stacking-fault energy.
Reduced stacking-fault energy stabilizes partial dislocations in CoCrFeNiTi.
Low stacking-fault energy can promote deformation modes that preserve ductility.
Short-range ordering lowers the barrier to dislocation motion in CoCrFeNiTi.
Short-range ordering and moderate stacking-fault energy facilitate both planar slip and cross slip in CoCrFeNiTi.
Easier dislocation motion causes lower work-hardening rates and moderate strength while preserving ductility and machinability.
Short-range ordering limits the strength and hardness of CoCrFeNiTi relative to alloys with stronger long-range order or higher fault energies.
Increasing short-range ordering will increase stacking-fault density in CoCrFeNiTi.
Increasing short-range ordering will increase planar-dislocation slip activity in CoCrFeNiTi.
Increasing short-range ordering will reduce the hardness of CoCrFeNiTi relative to a minimally ordered comparator.
More strongly ordered CoCrFeNiTi will retain higher ductility at both 25 °C and 600 °C.

The baseline solution-annealed CoCrFeNiTi has limited short-range order, moderate stacking-fault energy, moderately high ductility, and lower hardness and strength than other Ti-containing high-entropy alloys.
The hypothesis is limited to nominally single-phase near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi loaded in tension or compression from 25 °C to 600 °C at strain rates of 10^-4 to 10^-3 s^-1.
The proposed mechanism applies only in the absence of second-phase intermetallic precipitation or extensive chemical segregation.
Thermal treatments or changes in Ti/Co ratio can be used to create different degrees of short-range order for comparison.
